source_text: Quod licet, quantae sit profanitatis, vix indicatum iam vehementer appareat, tamen pace ipsius divinitatis, cuius aequitatem tuemur, quale sit hoc, vel levi discus sione videamus. Ut ipse itaque fiat legis suae praevaricator, rerum necessitate, quae eum premunt, an sua imbecillitate compellitur? An, quia horum neutrum est, sola libidine delinquendi? At hoc nec Manichaeus dicere potuit et ideo commentus est Deum vestrum grave proelium pertulisse.
pass_a_gloss: Although of how great a profanity this is, once indicated, already vehemently appears, nevertheless with the peace of the very divinity whose fairness we guard, let us see of what sort this is, even by a light discussion. That he himself therefore become a transgressor of his own law, is he compelled by the necessity of things which press him, or by his own weakness? Or, because neither of these is, by desire of doing wrong alone? But not even the Manichaean could say this, and therefore he invented that your god had endured a grave battle.

lemmas.lexica: Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil
LS libido; Blaise often sexual desire; Julian treats as created sensation, not a sin-nature
LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS lex; Blaise lex Dei / sacred Law

pass_b_english: Although the extent of this irreverence is glaringly obvious as soon as it is mentioned, let us—with the permission of the very God whose fairness we defend—consider its character, even through a brief examination. What forces him to become a violator of his own law: the pressure of circumstances that overwhelm him, or his own weakness? Or, since it is neither, is it simply a desire to do wrong? But even Mani could not say this, and so he invented a story that your god had endured a terrible battle.

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
